mainTopic: Doubled and single-word answers to a proposal of קידושין, and the laws of קידושין with a שטר
overview: The amud opens with three short stories. In each, a woman asks a man for something small, he asks whether she will be מקודשת with it, and she answers with a doubled word like "Give, give!" רב חמא and רב זביד rule that a doubled answer means nothing. On a single-word answer, רבינא says she is מקודשת and רב סמא בר רקתא swears she is not. The הלכה is that she is not מקודשת. The גמרא then gives final rulings on earlier cases: silk, רבי אלעזר, and רבא in the name of רב נחמן. Next a ברייתא teaches קידושין with a שטר, and רבי זירא בר ממל asks why the husband writes it when a seller writes a bill of sale. רבא first answers from the פסוקים, and after challenges he says it is a הלכה from tradition that is only leaned on the פסוקים. רב נחמן explains that the father's consent counts before she is a בוגרת and her own consent counts after. Finally ריש לקיש asks about a שטר אירוסין not written for her, and that question continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The glass beads story: "Give, give" means nothing
steps.stepSummary: A man is selling strings of glass beads. A woman asks for one string, and he asks whether she will be מקודשת with it. She answers "Give, give!" רב חמא rules that this answer means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: (A man was selling strings of) glass beads. A woman came and said to him: "Give me one string." He said to her: "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She said: "Give, give!" רב חמא said: any "Give, give" is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a story that began on the previous page and gives רב חמא's ruling: her doubled answer "Give, give" does not create קידושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The man made the gift depend on קידושין, so the whole question is whether she agreed to his condition. By repeating the word, she sounds like she is brushing him off ("sure, sure, just hand it over"). She is not really saying yes to marriage, so her answer counts as nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: You will be betrothed to me
It is nothing; it has no legal effect

phrases.english: glass beads.
phrases.notes: This finishes a sentence from the previous page: a certain man was selling strings of glass beads.

phrases.english: A certain woman came,
She said to him: "Give me one string."

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: ״אִי יָהֲבִינָא לִיךְ מִיקַּדְּשַׁתְּ לִי״?
phrases.english: He said to her: "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?"
She said to him: "Give, give!"
Rav Chama said:
Any "Give, give" is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חָמָא: כֹּל ״הַבָה מֵיהֲבָה״ לָאו כְּלוּם הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes a case story that started on the previous דף.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A woman who answers "Give, give" to a conditional proposal of קידושין is not מקודשת; the doubled phrase means nothing.

steps.title: The wine cup story: "Give me to drink" means nothing
steps.stepSummary: A man is drinking wine in a store. A woman asks for a cup, and he asks whether she will be מקודשת with it. She answers "Give to drink, give me to drink!" רב חמא again rules that this means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man was drinking wine in a store. A woman came and said: "Give me one cup." He said: "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She said: "Give to drink, give me to drink!" רב חמא said: any "Give to drink, give me to drink" is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a second story with the same pattern, and רב חמא gives the same ruling: no קידושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Only the item and the wording change: a cup of wine instead of beads, and "give me to drink" instead of "give." The doubled answer still sounds like she just wants the drink and is not taking his offer seriously. So the rule from the first story applies here too.

keyTerms.meaning: "Give to drink, give me to drink!" (doubled answer)

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה קָא שָׁתֵי חַמְרָא בְּחָנוּתָא.
phrases.english: There was a certain man who was drinking wine in a store.
A certain woman came,
She said to him: "Give me one cup."

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: ״אִי יָהֵיבְנָא לִיךְ מִיקַּדְּשַׁתְּ לִי״?
phrases.english: He said to her: "If I give it to you, will you be betrothed to me?"
She said to him: "Give to drink, give me to drink!"
Rav Chama said:
Any "Give to drink, give me to drink" is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה קָא שָׁתֵי חַמְרָא בְּחָנוּתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel case with the same pattern and the same ruling as step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The doubled answer "Give to drink, give me to drink" does not count as accepting קידושין.

steps.title: The dates story: "Throw, throw" means nothing
steps.stepSummary: A man is knocking dates down from a palm tree. A woman asks him to throw her two, and he asks whether she will be מקודשת with them. She answers "Throw, throw!" רב זביד rules that this means nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: A man was throwing dates down from a palm tree. A woman came and said: "Throw me two!" He said: "If I throw them to you, will you be betrothed to me?" She said: "Throw, throw!" רב זביד said: any "Throw, throw" is nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a third story with the same pattern, and this time רב זביד rules that the doubled answer means nothing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now a different אמורא, רב זביד, gives the same kind of ruling. Three stories with one rule show that this is a general principle: a doubled "just give it" answer is not agreement to קידושין. It also sets up the next question: what if she says the word only once?

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who rules in this story

steps.whatToRemember: In all three stories the answer was doubled ("Give, give" / "Give to drink, give me to drink" / "Throw, throw"), and in all three she is not מקודשת.

phrases.aramaic: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה קָא שָׁדֵי תַּמְרֵי מִדִּקְלָא.
phrases.english: There was a certain man who was throwing dates down from a palm tree.
A certain woman came,
She said to him: "Throw me two!"

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לַהּ: ״אִי שָׁדֵינָא לִיךְ מִיקַּדְּשַׁתְּ לִי״?
phrases.english: He said to her: "If I throw them to you, will you be betrothed to me?"
She said to him: "Throw, throw!"
Rav Zevid said:
Any "Throw, throw" is nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָהוּא גַּבְרָא דַּהֲוָה קָא שָׁדֵי תַּמְרֵי מִדִּקְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A third parallel case, ruled the same way by a different אמורא.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The doubled answer "Throw, throw" does not count as accepting קידושין.

steps.title: What if she answers with just one word?
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask what the law is if the woman answers with a single word, "Give," "Give to drink," or "Throw," without repeating it.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: if she said just "Give," "Give to drink," or "Throw," what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a new question and sets up the opinions that follow: is a single-word answer different from a doubled one?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The three stories only taught that a doubled answer means nothing. A single word sounds more like a plain request, as if she were saying "Yes, go ahead and give it on your terms." So it is unclear whether a single word counts as agreeing.

keyTerms.meaning: A question was asked among them (a real open question)

phrases.english: A question was raised before them:
"Give," "Give to drink," and "Throw": what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the three doubled-answer cases and asks about the undoubled version.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a single, undoubled answer ("Give," "Give to drink," "Throw") counts as accepting the man's condition of קידושין.

steps.title: רבינא: She is betrothed
steps.stepSummary: רבינא answers that with a single-word answer, she is מקודשת.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא gives the first answer to the question: a single-word answer does count, so the קידושין take effect.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבינא understands that without the doubling there is no sign of mocking. She heard his condition and said "Give," so it sounds like she is taking the item on his terms.

phrases.english: Ravina said: She is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: First answer to the question in step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A single-word answer counts as agreeing, so she is מקודשת.

steps.title: רב סמא בר רקתא swears: She is not betrothed
steps.stepSummary: רב סמא בר רקתא strongly disagrees with רבינא and swears "By the king's crown!" that she is not מקודשת.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב סמא בר רקתא said: By the king's crown! She is not betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives the opposite answer, and says it with a strong oath.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב סמא holds that even a single "Give" is just a request for the item. It is not a clear yes to marriage. The oath shows how sure he is of this.

keyTerms.meaning: The אמורא who disagrees with רבינא

phrases.english: Rav Sama bar Rakta said:
By the king's crown!
She is not betrothed.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב סַמָּא בַּר רַקְתָּא אָמַר: תָּגָא דְמַלְכָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite answer to רבינא's.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Even a single-word answer is not acceptance, so she is not מקודשת.

steps.title: The הלכה: She is not betrothed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules like רב סמא בר רקתא: even with a single-word answer, she is not מקודשת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And the הלכה is: she is not betrothed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the argument and gives the final law: she is not מקודשת.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The הלכה follows רב סמא בר רקתא. A short reply like "Give" is not clear enough to count as agreeing to קידושין, whether she says it once or twice.
steps.whatToRemember: Doubled answer: not מקודשת (רב חמא, רב זביד). Single-word answer: argued between רבינא and רב סמא בר רקתא. The הלכה is that she is not מקודשת either way.
steps.whyThisMatters: For קידושין to take effect, the woman must clearly agree. A casual "just give it" reply, said once or twice, is not enough.

phrases.english: And the halakha is: She is not betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Decides the argument between steps 5 and 6.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Even a single-word answer like "Give" does not count as accepting קידושין; she is not מקודשת.

steps.title: Three final rulings on the earlier cases
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules that silk needs no appraisal, and that the הלכה follows רבי אלעזר and follows רבא in the name of רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: The הלכה is that silk does not need to be appraised. The הלכה follows רבי אלעזר, and the הלכה follows what רבא said in the name of רב נחמן.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is closing the earlier discussions by stating which way the הלכה goes in three cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each ruling settles an earlier discussion from the previous amud. Silk can be used for קידושין without first having its value checked. In the case of a man who promised a large sum, רבי אלעזר's view is accepted, and so is רב נחמן's ruling as reported by רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: Appraisal, having the item's value checked

steps.whatToRemember: These three lines are final rulings. They close the earlier section before the גמרא starts the topic of קידושין with a שטר.

phrases.english: And the halacha is: silk garments do not need appraisal.
And the halacha is like Rabbi Elazar,
phrases.notes: This is his earlier case: a man promised one hundred דינרים, gave only one, and she is still מקודשת.

phrases.english: And the halacha is like Rava, who said in the name of Rav Nachman.
phrases.notes: This is the earlier case where he promised one hundred and gave a pledge instead. That is not a valid קידושין.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Wraps up earlier cases from the previous amud (silk, the hundred-דינר promise, the pledge) with final rulings, after the single-word-answer question was settled in step 7.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Silk needs no appraisal. The הלכה follows רבי אלעזר, and follows רבא in the name of רב נחמן.

steps.title: How קידושין works with a document
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that if a man writes "Your daughter is מקודשת to me" on paper or a shard and gives it to the father, she is מקודשת, even if the material is worth less than a פרוטה.
steps.simpleTranslation: The רבנן taught: How does קידושין work through a שטר? If he wrote to the father, on paper or on a clay shard, "Your daughter is מקודשת to me," or "Your daughter is מאורסת to me," or "Your daughter is mine as a wife," she is מקודשת. This is true even if the paper or shard is not worth a פרוטה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: the second way of doing קידושין, through a written document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With money, the item has to be worth at least a פרוטה. Here the ברייתא says the paper's value does not matter, because the words written on it are what make the קידושין work. Any of the three wordings works.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth at least a פרוטה, the smallest coin

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think the paper is acting like money here. Its value doesn't matter at all. The written words are what make the קידושין.

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught: With a document, how does it work?

phrases.aramaic: כָּתַב לוֹ עַל הַנְּיָיר אוֹ עַל הַחֶרֶס,
phrases.english: He wrote for him on paper or on a clay shard,
phrases.notes: "For him" means for the girl's father.

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שָׁוֶה פְרוּטָה,
phrases.english: even though it is not worth a peruta,
"Your daughter is betrothed to me,"
"Your daughter is betrothed to me,"
"Your daughter is mine as a wife" —
she is betrothed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a fresh topic, קידושין with a document, after the rulings on קידושין with money.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A document from the man saying "Your daughter is מקודשת to me" works, even if the material is worth less than a פרוטה.

steps.title: Why does the husband write, when in a sale the seller writes?
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא בר ממל objects that this document doesn't match a bill of sale. In a sale the seller writes, but here the husband, who is like the buyer, writes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא בר ממל challenged it: This document isn't like a bill of sale! There, the seller writes "My field is sold to you." Here, the husband writes "Your daughter is מקודשת to me"!
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא בר ממל attacks the ברייתא's wording by comparing it to a sale document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He assumes the document should work like a bill of sale. In a sale, the one giving something up, the seller, writes it. In this ברייתא, though, the husband is the one receiving, yet he is the one who writes. That seems backwards.

phrases.aramaic: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא בַּר מֶמֶל:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira bar Memel challenged it:

phrases.aramaic: הָא לָא דָּמֵי הַאי שְׁטָרָא לִשְׁטַר זְבִינֵי!
phrases.english: But this document is not like a bill of sale!

phrases.aramaic: הָתָם, מוֹכֵר כּוֹתֵב לוֹ ״שָׂדִי מְכוּרָה לָךְ״,
phrases.english: There, the seller writes to him, "My field is sold to you,"
here, the husband writes, "Your daughter is betrothed to me"!

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא בַּר מֶמֶל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the ברייתא in step 9 over who writes the document.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא's statement that the husband writes the document
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A sale document is written by the seller. The husband is like the buyer, so he should not be the one writing.

steps.title: Each document follows its own פסוק
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that each document follows the wording of its own פסוק. For a sale, the פסוק makes the seller the one who acts. For marriage, the פסוק makes the husband the one who acts.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: There, the wording comes from the context of the פסוק, and here too the wording comes from the context of the פסוק. There it says "And he sells of his land," so the תורה made it depend on the seller. Here it says "If a man takes," so the תורה made it depend on the husband.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers רבי זירא's question by showing that each case follows its own פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The two documents don't have to match each other. Each one follows how the תורה describes that act. In a sale, the תורה describes the seller acting ("he sells"). In marriage, it describes the husband acting ("he takes"), so the husband writes.

keyTerms.meaning: From the context of the פסוק
The תורה made it depend on
If a man takes, the פסוק about marriage

steps.whatToRemember: רבא's first answer: each document follows its own פסוק, so the husband writes because the תורה says "כי יקח". Watch how this answer is challenged in steps 12-14 and replaced in step 15.
steps.whyThisMatters: It gives a first explanation for why the husband writes the שטר of קידושין while the seller writes a sale document. The rule itself stays, even after the explanation is replaced in step 15.

phrases.english: Rava said: There, it comes from the context of the verse,
and here, it comes from the context of the verse.
There it is written, "And he sells of his ancestral land" —
the Torah made it depend on the seller,
here it is written, "If a man takes" —
the Torah made it depend on the husband.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא בר ממל's challenge in step 10.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishes the two cases, since each follows its own פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The קידושין document should match a bill of sale, so the giver (the father) should write it.
steps.terutzMaskana: Each document follows its own פסוק. The תורה puts the sale on the seller and the marriage on the husband, so the husband writes.

steps.title: A sale verse seems to make the buyer act
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא: a פסוק in ירמיהו about sales speaks of the buyers acting, not the seller.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, by a sale, it is also written: "Fields shall they buy for money"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבא's answer from step 11. It brings a פסוק about sales where the buyer, not the seller, is the one acting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said a sale document is written by the seller because the פסוק makes the seller act. But "יִקְנוּ" means "they will buy," which points to the buyer. So the פסוקים about sale do not clearly point to the seller.

keyTerms.meaning: There, meaning the case of a sale

phrases.english: There too it is written:
"Fields shall they buy for money"!

steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the sale פסוק makes the seller the one who acts
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A different sale פסוק uses a word that makes the buyer the one who acts

steps.title: Read the word as the seller transferring
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers by reading the word with different vowels so that it means "they will transfer ownership," which is what the seller does.
steps.simpleTranslation: Read it as "יַקְנוּ": they will cause others to acquire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רבא by changing how the word is read. The new reading makes the seller the one acting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With one vowel changed, "יִקְנוּ" (they will buy) becomes "יַקְנוּ" (they will give ownership). Read this way, the פסוק talks about sellers again, so רבא's rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Read it as, meaning read the word in a different way
They will transfer ownership, as a seller does

phrases.english: Read into it "yaknu" (they will transfer ownership).

steps.terutzResolutionType: Re-reading the word in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק says the buyers act
steps.terutzMaskana: Read differently, the פסוק says the sellers transfer ownership

steps.title: The same re-reading trick works against marriage
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why we re-read the sale word. If it is to match the תורה's "and he sells," then we could also re-read the marriage word to match "I gave my daughter," and then the father would be the one who acts.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the reason you read it as "יַקְנוּ"? Because it is written "and he sells." So too, read "כי יקח" as "when he is given," since it is written "I gave my daughter to this man."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer of step 13. If we may change vowels to make one פסוק match another, we can do the same for marriage, and that would break רבא's rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The re-reading in step 13 was done so the פסוק would match "וּמָכַר," which shows the seller acting. But a different marriage פסוק says the father gave his daughter. By the same method, "כִּי יִקַּח" could be re-read to mean the husband is given the woman. Then the father, who is like the seller, would be the actor, and the husband should not be the one who writes.

keyTerms.meaning: "When a man takes," the marriage פסוק

phrases.english: What is the reason you read it as "yaknu"?
Because it is written "and he sells"
So too, read into it "ki yakach" (when he is given to take)
phrases.notes: The normal reading in דברים 22:13 is "כִּי יִקַּח", "when a man takes." The changed vowel makes the husband the one who receives.

phrases.english: as it is written: "I gave my daughter to this man."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the re-reading answer of step 13
steps.kashyaTarget: The method of re-reading a פסוק to match another פסוק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The same method applied to marriage would make the father the actor, which undoes רבא's distinction

steps.title: These rules are a tradition, only leaned on פסוקים
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives a new answer: who writes each document is a הלכה from tradition, and the רבנן only attached it to the פסוקים as a support.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: They are a הלכה, and the רבנן leaned them on the פסוקים.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא drops the attempt to prove the rules from the פסוקים. He says the rules come from tradition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the rules come from tradition, it does not matter that the פסוקים can be read more than one way. The פסוקים serve only as a support, an אסמכתא, and are not the real source. So the challenges from the wording of the פסוקים no longer hurt the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, which signals a new answer replacing the old one
They are a הלכה, a law received by tradition
They leaned them on, a support rather than a true source

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
They are a halacha (from tradition)
and the Rabbis leaned them on the verses.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the source-based answer that step 14 knocked down
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the source from the פסוק to tradition
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The rules about who writes are proven from the wording of the פסוקים
steps.terutzMaskana: The rules are a received הלכה; the פסוקים are only a support
steps.whatToRemember: Who writes the document (seller in a sale, husband in קידושין) is a received הלכה. The פסוקים are only leaned on as a support.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the הלכה changed. Only the source changed. The husband still writes the קידושין document.

steps.title: Even the sale verse shows the buyer only receives
steps.stepSummary: A second answer: the same section in ירמיהו says "I took the deed of purchase," which shows the buyer receives a document that the seller wrote.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you want, say: there too it is written, "And I took the deed of purchase."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives another way to answer the challenge of step 12. It stays with the פסוקים and shows that the buyer only takes the document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In ירמיהו the buyer says "I took" the deed, meaning it was handed to him. So the seller is the one who wrote and gave it. This fits רבא's original rule, and there is no need for the re-reading that failed in step 14.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say: an alternative answer

phrases.english: And if you want, say:
there too it is written:
phrases.notes: "There" means the same section in ירמיהו that step 12 quoted.

phrases.english: "And I took the deed of purchase."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second answer to the challenge of step 12, alongside step 15
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings another פסוק from the same context
steps.terutzMaskana: ירמיהו shows the buyer receiving a deed written by the seller
steps.whatToRemember: Two answers: either the rules are a tradition with the פסוקים as support, or ירמיהו itself shows the seller wrote and the buyer took the deed.

steps.title: A document given for a girl who is not yet a בוגרת
steps.stepSummary: רבא in the name of רב נחמן: if he writes "Your daughter is מקודשת to me" on paper or a shard, she is מקודשת with the father's consent, whether it was given to the father or to her, as long as she is not yet a בוגרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבא said in the name of רב נחמן: If he wrote for him on paper or a shard, even if it is not worth a פרוטה, "Your daughter is מקודשת to me," "Your daughter is betrothed to me," or "Your daughter is mine as a wife," whether through her father or through herself, she is מקודשת with his (the father's) consent, provided she has not become a בוגרת.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ruling about the קידושין document. It explains whose consent counts when the girl is still under her father's authority.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן repeats the ברייתא's case from step 9, with the same three wordings, and adds two new details. The document may be handed to the father or to the girl. But the father's consent is what makes it work, because before she is a בוגרת, her קידושין belongs to her father.

keyTerms.meaning: Worth a פרוטה, the smallest coin
She became a בוגרת, a fully adult woman

phrases.english: And Rava said in the name of Rav Nachman:

phrases.aramaic: כָּתַב לוֹ עַל הַנְּיָיר אוֹ עַל הַחֶרֶס
phrases.english: If he wrote for him on paper or on a shard,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שָׁוֶה פְרוּטָה
phrases.english: even though it is not worth a peruta:
"Your daughter is mekudeshet to me,"
"Your daughter is betrothed to me,"
"Your daughter is mine as a wife,"

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין עַל יְדֵי אָבִיהָ בֵּין עַל יְדֵי עַצְמָהּ
phrases.english: whether through her father or through herself,
she is mekudeshet with his consent,
provided that she has not become a bogeret.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the ברייתא of step 9 and adds new details
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A girl who is not yet a בוגרת is מקודשת through a document with her father's consent, whether it was handed to him or to her
steps.confusionAlert: "Through herself" does not mean her own consent counts here. It only means she can be the one who receives the document. The father's consent is what makes the קידושין work.

steps.title: A document given to a woman who is a בוגרת
steps.stepSummary: If he writes to her "You are מקודשת to me" on paper or a shard, she is מקודשת whether it was given through her father or to her, with her own consent, as long as she is a בוגרת.
steps.simpleTranslation: If he wrote for her on paper or a shard, even if it is not worth a פרוטה, "You are מקודשת to me," "You are mine as a wife," or "You are betrothed to me," she is מקודשת, whether through her father or through herself, with her consent, provided she is a בוגרת.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of רב נחמן's ruling. It covers a woman who is an adult and controls her own קידושין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the wording speaks to her directly ("You are..."). Once she is a בוגרת, her own consent is what counts, even if the document passes through her father's hands. This mirrors step 17, where the father's consent counted.

keyTerms.meaning: Behold you are, which speaks directly to the woman
A fully adult woman, no longer under her father's authority for קידושין

phrases.aramaic: כָּתַב לָהּ עַל הַנְּיָיר אוֹ עַל הַחֶרֶס
phrases.english: If he wrote for her on paper or on a shard,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שָׁוֶה פְרוּטָה
phrases.english: even though it is not worth a peruta:
"You are mekudeshet to me,"
"You are mine as a wife,"
"You are betrothed to me,"

phrases.aramaic: מְקוּדֶּשֶׁת, בֵּין עַל יְדֵי אָבִיהָ, בֵּין עַל יְדֵי עַצְמָהּ
phrases.english: she is mekudeshet, whether through her father or through herself,
with her consent, provided that she has become a bogeret.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּתַב לָהּ עַל הַנְּיָיר אוֹ עַל הַחֶרֶס
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The matching second case of רב נחמן's ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A בוגרת is מקודשת through a document with her own consent, whether it is handed to her or passes through her father
steps.whatToRemember: The key question is whose consent counts. Before she is a בוגרת, it is the father's. Once she is a בוגרת, it is her own. Who physically receives the document does not matter.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that in קידושין the authority to agree, not the hand that receives the document, is what decides whether the קידושין works.

steps.title: A betrothal document not written for her
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן לקיש asks whether a שטר אירוסין that was not written for this specific woman is valid. The גמרא begins the first side of the question: maybe we compare entering marriage (הויות) to leaving marriage (יציאות).
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן לקיש asked: If a betrothal document was written not for her sake, what is the law? Do we compare the ways of becoming married to the ways of leaving a marriage? Just as...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question about a שטר אירוסין that was written without this woman in mind. It then starts to set up the first possible answer, and the sentence continues in the next part.
steps.deeperAnalysis: So far we learned that a man can marry a woman with a שטר. Now ריש לקיש asks whether that שטר must be written specifically for her. The first side of the question suggests a היקש, a comparison between entering marriage and leaving it. If they are compared, the rules for a גט might also apply to a שטר אירוסין.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked. This word opens a real question where the answer is not yet known.
A betrothal document. It is one of the ways to make a woman מקודשת.
Not for her sake. The document was written without this particular woman in mind.
Becomings. These are the ways a woman enters marriage.
Leavings. These are the ways a woman leaves marriage, such as a גט.
We compare (make a היקש). The גמרא is asking whether one set of rules is linked to the other.

steps.confusionAlert: The words 'הויות ליציאות מקשינן' are not the final answer. They are only the first side of ריש לקיש's question, and the sentence is cut off at 'מה'.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish asked:
A document of betrothal
that he wrote not for her sake, what is the law?
Do we compare the ways of entering marriage to the ways of leaving it?
Just as...

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Steps 17 and 18 established that a שטר written on paper or a shard can make a woman מקודשת. This step asks a new question: must that שטר be written specifically for her?
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a שטר אירוסין valid if it was written not for this specific woman? The first side asks whether we compare entering marriage to leaving it.
steps.whyThisMatters: It begins a discussion of whether the rules for writing a שטר אירוסין follow the rules for writing a גט.
